levels.xor.description:

home.titleC: build all the way to GPT.
home.lead: Each level asks you to wire existing parts into a new one, which then joins your library. Sigmoid and softmax first, then backpropagation, optimizers and attention, and finally a GPT you train in the browser and that writes text.
chapter.0.desc: add, mul, exp, log → sigmoid, tanh
chapter.1.desc: Build derivative circuits, then let them calculate how to adjust parameters.
chapter.2.desc: Broadcasting, Matrix multiply, Softmax, Layer normalization
chapter.3.desc: A model's answer computed from its inputs is a prediction. A loss compares that prediction with the correct answer; training adjusts parameters to reduce the loss.
chapter.4.desc: Number characters, turn them into vectors, then predict the next character. Training changes parameters; generation only uses them.
chapter.5.desc: See where fixed windows fail, carry state with an RNN, then let attention look back before forecasting.
chapter.6.desc: Let positions find and mix relevant content, then use it to predict the next character.
chapter.7.desc: Stack information exchange and per-position processing into a GPT-style character predictor: train against known answers, then generate one character at a time.

levels.0-1.title: Negate
levels.0-1.description:
Negation turns an increase into a decrease.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $y=−x$, its sign reversed. A scalar is one number.
levels.0-2.title: Subtract
levels.0-2.description:
Subtraction measures a difference.
This level: input scalars $a$ and $b$; output their difference, scalar $y=a−b$.
levels.0-4.title: Divide
levels.0-4.description:
Division compares quantities as a ratio.
This level: input scalar $a$ and nonzero scalar $b$ (both may be negative); output quotient scalar $y=a/b$.
levels.0-5.title: Sigmoid
levels.0-5.description:
Networks need nonlinear functions to model curved relationships.
Sigmoid maps real numbers into (0, 1).
This level: input scalar $x$; output activation scalar $y=σ(x)=1/(1+e⁻ˣ)$.
levels.0-6.title: Hyperbolic tangent
levels.0-6.description:
Tanh centers activation.
This level: scalar $x$ in; activation scalar $y=tanh(x)=(eˣ−e⁻ˣ)/(eˣ+e⁻ˣ)$ out.
levels.0-7.title: ReLU
levels.0-7.description:
ReLU is the most common activation function: negative numbers become 0, and positive numbers stay the same. This level introduces a new component, Maximum, which outputs the larger of two numbers. Comparing two numbers can't be built from addition, subtraction, multiplication or division, so Maximum is provided as a basic component.
This level: input scalar $x$; output $y=max(x,0)$.
levels.0-8.title: Square root
levels.0-8.description: This level: scalar $x>0$ in; root scalar $y=√x$ out.
levels.1-1.title: Derivative of a square
levels.1-1.description:
A derivative is the slope at an input, not the function value.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $f′(x)$.
The original function:

$$
f(x)=x²
$$
levels.1-2.title: Product rule
levels.1-2.description:
A product depends on both factors.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $f′(x)$, the slope of $f$.
The original function:

$$
f(x)=x·eˣ
$$
levels.1-3.title: Chain rule
levels.1-3.description:
Nested functions pass changes through each layer.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $f′(x)$, the slope of $f$.
The original function:

$$
f(x)=e³ˣ
$$
levels.1-4.title: Derivative of log
levels.1-4.description:
Logarithms turn products into sums; this derivative returns later in cross entropy.
This level: input positive scalar $x$; output scalar $f′(x)$, the slope of $f$.
The original function:

$$
f(x)=ln(x)
$$
levels.1-5.title: Derivative of sigmoid
levels.1-5.description:
This derivative will pass changes back to the input during training.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $σ′(x)$, the rate of change of the Sigmoid function $σ(x)$.
In case you forgot, Sigmoid is:

$$
σ(x)=1/(1+e⁻ˣ)
$$
levels.1-6.title: Derivative of tanh
levels.1-6.description:
Learn this derivative to prepare for training networks.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $tanh′(x)$, the rate of change of $tanh(x)$.
In case you forgot, Tanh is:

$$
tanh(x)=(eˣ−e⁻ˣ)/(eˣ+e⁻ˣ)
$$
levels.1-7.title: Log chain rule
levels.1-7.description:
Apply the chain rule to a logarithm containing a square.
This level: input scalar $x$; output scalar $f′(x)$, the slope of $f$.
The original function:

$$
f(x)=ln(1+x²)
$$

levels.xor.hint1: Use a hidden layer to form nonlinear features, then a second layer for class probabilities. Linear layers alone cannot separate XOR.
levels.xor.hint2: Use random weights [2,8], [8,2], biases [8], [2]; Sigmoid between layers, Softmax last.
levels.0-1.hint1: Negation turns an increase into a decrease. What multiplier reverses the sign of $x$? For example, 3 becomes −3.
levels.0-1.hint2: Set Constant to −1, feed it and $x$ into Multiply, then connect the result to $y$. Edit the constant in Attributes.
levels.0-2.hint1: Subtraction measures errors or gaps. Subtracting a number means adding its what? For example, $5−2=3$.
levels.0-2.hint2: Feed $b$ into Negate, then feed its result and $a$ into Add. Connect the result to $y$.
levels.square.title: Square
levels.square.description:
Squaring turns negatives positive and magnifies large errors; mean squared error and variance both use it later.
This level: input scalar $x$, output $y=x²$.
levels.square.hint1: $x²=x·x$, but there is only one $x$. One output can feed several wires: try dragging two wires out of $x$.
levels.square.hint2: Connect $x$ to both the $a$ and $b$ inputs of Multiply, and the result to $y$. For example, $x=−3$ gives $y=9$.
levels.0-4.hint1: Division computes ratios. Dividing by $b$ means multiplying by its what? $a$ may be negative, so do not take its logarithm.
levels.0-4.hint2: Feed $b$ into Reciprocal, then multiply its result by $a$ using Multiply. For $a=6$ and $b=−2$, $y=−3$.
levels.0-5.hint1: $σ$ denotes Sigmoid; $e$ is the base of natural exponentials. Activations let networks express nonlinear relationships. Start with the innermost $−x$.
levels.0-5.hint2: Use Negate, then Exponential; Add the constant 1 and finish with Reciprocal. At $x=0$, $y=0.5$.
levels.0-6.hint1: Tanh, the hyperbolic tangent, maps reals into (−1, 1), a zero-centered activation. $e$ is the natural exponential base. Try multiplying numerator and denominator by $eˣ$.
levels.0-6.hint2: Use Multiply and Exponential to get $u=e²ˣ$, then Subtract, Add and Divide for $(u−1)/(u+1)$. Reuse the output of $u$ with multiple wires. At $x=0$, $y=0$.
levels.0-7.hint1: ReLU is an activation that keeps positive values. What should you compare $x$ with to remove negative values?
levels.0-7.hint2: Feed $x$ and a Constant set to 0 into Maximum. For example, −2 becomes 0, while 3 stays 3.
levels.0-8.hint1: A square root restores the units of a squared quantity. $√x$ is the positive square root, or $x$ to the power $\frac{1}{2}$; for example, $√9=3$.
levels.0-8.hint2: The natural logarithm turns powers into multiplication: $√x=exp(0.5·ln(x))$. Connect Logarithm, Multiply by a Constant of 0.5, then Exponential.
levels.1-1.hint1: $f$ denotes a function; a prime $′$ means its derivative with respect to the input. The power rule is $(xⁿ)′=n·xⁿ⁻¹$, with fixed exponent $n$.
levels.1-1.hint2: Use Multiply with $x$ and a Constant of 2. At $x=3$, the function value is 9, but the required slope is 6.
levels.1-2.hint1: Product rule: $(u·v)′=u′·v+u·v′$, where $u$ and $v$ are functions of $x$. Here $u=x$ and $v=eˣ$; $e$ is the natural exponential base.
levels.1-2.hint2: The derivatives of $x$ and $eˣ$ are 1 and $eˣ$. Factor to get $eˣ·(1+x)$ using Exponential, Add and Multiply. At $x=0$, output 1.
levels.1-3.hint1: The chain rule handles nested functions: multiply the outer derivative, evaluated at the inner value, by the inner derivative. Here the inner value is $u=3x$ and the outer function is $eᵘ$; $e$ is the natural exponential base.
levels.1-3.hint2: The outer derivative is $eᵘ$ and the inner derivative is 3. Multiply $x$ by 3, apply Exponential, then Multiply by 3. At $x=0$, output 3.
levels.1-4.hint1: $ln$ is the natural logarithm; the prime means differentiate with respect to $x$. Logarithms compress numeric ranges. If $u=ln(x)$, then $x=eᵘ$. Try differentiating both sides.
levels.1-4.hint2: From $1=eᵘ·u′$, obtain $u′=1/x$. Feed $x$ into Reciprocal; at $x=2$, the slope is 0.5.
levels.1-5.hint1: $σ$ denotes Sigmoid and $σ′$ its derivative, used to pass rates of change back to the input. Differentiate $σ(x)=(1+e⁻ˣ)⁻¹$ by the chain rule, then rewrite using $σ(x)$ alone.
levels.1-5.hint2: $σ′(x)=σ(x)·(1−σ(x))$. Use Sigmoid once, then Subtract and Multiply; at $x=0$, output 0.25. Passing unlocks the Sigmoid derivative part.
levels.1-6.hint1: $tanh$ is the hyperbolic tangent; the prime denotes its derivative, used to pass rates of change to a preceding layer. Write it as numerator $u$ over denominator $v$ and use $(u/v)′=(u′v−uv′)/v²$.
levels.1-6.hint2: $tanh′(x)=1−tanh(x)²$. Use Tanh once, Multiply its output by itself, then Subtract from 1. At $x=0$, output 1. Passing unlocks Tanh derivative.
levels.1-7.hint1: $ln$ is the natural logarithm. Since $1+x²$ is always positive, $x$ may have either sign. The outer $ln(u)$ has derivative $1/u$; the inner value is $u=1+x²$.
levels.1-7.hint2: The inner derivative is $2x$, giving $2x/(1+x²)$. Build it with Multiply, Add and Divide. At $x=1$, output 1.

levels.axes.title: Shapes and axes
levels.axes.description:
Task: use exactly one Sum node to sum every given 2D tensor row by row. Add the numbers in each row and output one number per row.
In the current example, input $x$ has shape [2×3] (2 rows of 3 numbers), so the row-sum output has shape [2]. The “Test shape” buttons also try [4×3], [2×5], and [3×1]. The task does not change: the output length always equals the row count.
Each direction of a tensor is an axis. Axis −1 means the last axis—the direction across each row—so summing axis −1 works for different row and column counts.
levels.axes.hint1: Connect $x$ → Sum → Row sums. You need exactly one Sum node.
levels.axes.hint2: Set the axis to −1 and turn off “Keep dimensions.” Then [4×3] → [4] and [2×5] → [2]: one number for each row.
levels.2-2.title: Broadcasting
levels.2-2.description:
Broadcasting combines different shapes entry by entry. Align from the last axis: lengths must match or one must be 1; missing leading axes count as 1. A length-1 axis reuses its value.
This level: scale rows, then add column offsets: inputs are data $x$ [4,3], row scales $s$ [4,1], column biases $b$ [3]; output the scaled and biased values $x ⊙ s + b$ [4,3]. Here $⊙$ means element-wise multiplication with broadcasting, not matrix multiplication; matrix multiplication is introduced in a later level.
levels.2-2.hint1: No new part needed: Add and element-wise Multiply both broadcast. Do not use Matrix multiply here.
levels.2-2.hint2: Use element-wise Multiply for $x ⊙ s$ (broadcasting $s$), then Add $b$, which broadcasts too.
levels.2-6.title: Transpose, then multiply
levels.2-6.description:
Compare two sets of row vectors by pairing every row with every row of the other set. Transpose swaps the last two axes; $bᵀ$ means transposed $b$, leaving batch axes unchanged.
This level: inputs $a$ [4,3], $b$ [5,3] hold row vectors; output pairwise dot products $a·bᵀ$ [4,5].
levels.2-6.hint1: Turn $b$ into [3×5], then use the matrix multiplication you built.
levels.2-6.hint2: Use Transpose with axes [−2,−1] into Matrix multiply’s $b$ port; wire $a$ to its $a$ port.
levels.2-1.title: Dot product
levels.2-1.description:
A dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them up, useful for weighted scores. Tests also use shorter vectors.
This level: input vectors $a$ and $b$ are both [6]; the dot-product output is scalar: $a·b$, a single number.
levels.2-1.hint1: Wire $a$ and $b$ straight into a multiply. You still get a list of 6.
levels.2-1.hint2: Sum along axis −1 with “Keep dimensions” off. The vector’s only axis is summed away, so the output is a scalar—a single number.
levels.2-3.title: Mean
levels.2-3.description:
A mean summarizes a row by dividing its sum by its count. Reduce only the last axis and keep it. Tests also use [3,5] and [2,3,4], so do not hard-code division by 6. This level provides Dimension size, which directly reads how many elements a chosen axis contains.
This level: input data $x$ [4,6]; output row means [4,1].
levels.2-3.hint1: Sum the last axis and keep its dimension; then use Dimension size to read the number of elements on that same axis. Axis −1 always means the last axis.
levels.2-3.hint2: Wire $x$ to Sum (axis −1, keep dimensions) and Dimension size (axis −1), then divide the sum by the dimension size. The scalar count broadcasts across every row.
levels.2-4.title: Outer product
levels.2-4.description:
An outer product lists every pairwise product, not just matching positions. Row $i$, column $j$ contains $aᵢ × bⱼ$, where $i$ and $j$ index the two lists. Insert length-1 axes so broadcasting can build the table.
This level: input vectors $a$ [4], $b$ [3]; output the outer product [4,3], holding all pairwise products.
levels.2-4.hint1: Insert dimension adds a length-1 axis where you choose. Stand $a$ up as a column and lay $b$ down as a row.
levels.2-4.hint2: Insert at axis −1 for $a$ and axis 0 for $b$, then multiply.
levels.2-5.title: Matrix multiplication
levels.2-5.description:
Matrix multiplication computes many dot products: result row $i$, column $j$ pairs row $i$ of the left matrix with column $j$ of the right. Broadcast to form entrywise products, then sum the shared-length axis. Tests add a batch axis, so count axes from the end.
This level: inputs are left matrix $a$ [4,3], right matrix $b$ [3,5]; output their matrix product [4,5].
levels.2-5.hint1: Aim for a [4×3×5] block of products: $a$ becomes [4×3×1] and $b$ becomes [1×3×5].
levels.2-5.hint2: Insert at axis −1 for $a$ and axis −3 for $b$. Multiply, then sum over axis −2 without keeping it.
levels.2-7.title: Softmax
levels.2-7.description:
Softmax converts scores to positive probabilities summing to 1 per row: exponentiate, then divide by the row total. Avoid overflow. The visualization below expands the current test data row by row through shifting, exponentiation and normalization.
This level: input scores $x$ [4,6]; output probabilities [4,6], each row summing to 1. Computers store numbers with finite precision: this number format cannot hold a value as large as $e^{100}$. Mathematically equal formulas may differ in computational reliability.
levels.2-7.hint1: Subtracting the same constant from a whole row doesn't change Softmax. Which constant is safest?
levels.2-7.hint2: Subtract Reduce maximum on the last axis, keeping dimensions. Apply Exponential; divide by its last-axis Sum, keeping dimensions.
levels.2-8.title: Layer norm
levels.2-8.description:
Layer normalization stabilizes later calculations; it does not produce probabilities. Subtract each row’s mean, then divide by the square root of its variance plus stabilizer $ε = 0.00001$. Constant rows become zero. The visualization below shows how the current row is centered, squared and scaled.
This level: input features $x$ [4,8]; output normalized features [4,8].
levels.2-8.hint1: Variance is the mean of the squared distance from the mean. Epsilon avoids division by zero on constant rows; this component has no extra trainable scale or bias.
ui.tensorProbeHelp: Tensor inputs are read-only. Switch cases to see other data. Hover a node for its full values.
levels.1-8.title: Partial derivatives
levels.1-8.description:
With several inputs, isolate the effect of changing just one.
This level: input scalars $a$, $b$; output scalar $∂f/∂a$, the rate of change as only $a$ varies. Hold $b$ fixed.
The original function:

$$
f(a,b)=a·b+eᵃ
$$
levels.1-8.hint1: $∂f/∂a$ is a partial derivative: it isolates the effect of one input changing. $eᵃ$ is the natural exponential. If $b$ stays fixed, what is the slope of $a·b$?
levels.1-8.hint2: The derivative of $a·b$ with respect to $a$ is $b$; the exponential is its own derivative. Use Exponential and Add for $b+eᵃ$. At $a=0$, $b=2$, output 3.
levels.1-9.title: Another direction
levels.1-9.description:
Practise holding one input fixed while differentiating with respect to another.
This level: input scalars $a$, $b$; output scalar $∂f/∂b$, the rate of change as only $b$ varies. Hold $a$ fixed.
The original function:

$$
f(a,b)=a·eᵃᵇ
$$
levels.1-9.hint1: $∂f/∂b$ measures how $f$ changes as only $b$ varies, with $a$ held fixed. The partial derivatives in every input direction form the gradient vector. Let $u=a·b$; first find the inner derivative $∂u/∂b$.
levels.1-9.hint2: $∂u/∂b=a$. By the chain rule, $∂eᵘ/∂b=eᵘ·a$; multiplying by the original function’s coefficient $a$ gives $∂f/∂b=a²·eᵘ$. First use Multiply for $u=a·b$, feed it into Exponential, then multiply by two copies of $a$. At $a=2$, $b=0$, output 4.
levels.1-10.title: Gradient on a surface
levels.1-10.description:
The previous two levels found the function's partial derivatives along the $a$ and $b$ directions. Put them in input order to form the gradient vector: $∇f=(∂f/∂a,∂f/∂b)$. The first component says how the function changes when only $a$ changes; the second says the same for $b$.
The gradient can be drawn as an arrow in the input plane. It points toward the fastest local increase in the function value; it is not the surface normal. In the plot, yellow is the target gradient and cyan is your gradient; a match turns green.
This level: input scalars $a$, $b$; output $∂a=∂f/∂a$ and $∂b=∂f/∂b$. Move the input or rotate the view to watch the gradient change.
The original function:

$$
f(a,b)=a·b+eᵃ
$$
levels.1-10.hint1: Reuse the first output from 1-8: $∂f/∂a=b+eᵃ$. For the other output, vary only $b$; then $a$ is constant.
levels.1-10.hint2: $∂f/∂b=a$. Connect $b+eᵃ$ to $∂a$ and connect $a$ directly to $∂b$. Together they form $∇f=(b+eᵃ,a)$.
levels.1-11.title: Backpropagation by hand
levels.1-11.description:
Earlier levels started with a function and differentiated it. Backpropagation instead receives a gradient from a later node, then carries it back through the computation graph to every input.
The forward calculation here has two steps:

$$
z=w·x+b
$$

$$
f=σ(z)
$$

The outer Sigmoid (or later computation) has already sent the upstream gradient to the intermediate value $z$:

$$
g=\frac{∂f}{∂z}
$$

This level starts there: backpropagate only through $z=w·x+b$, without recomputing Sigmoid. Carry $g$ back to $w$, $x$, and $b$.
This level: input scalars $w$, $x$, and $∂f/∂z$; output scalars $∂f/∂w$, $∂f/∂x$, and $∂f/∂b$. The value of $b$ is deliberately not provided; inspect $z=w·x+b$ and decide whether its value is actually needed during backpropagation.
levels.1-11.hint1: For each $q∈{w,x,b}$, apply the chain rule: $∂f/∂q=(∂f/∂z)·(∂z/∂q)$. The first factor is the supplied upstream gradient $g$; now differentiate $z=w·x+b$ with respect to $w$, $x$, and $b$ separately.
levels.1-11.hint2: $∂z/∂w=x$, $∂z/∂x=w$, and $∂z/∂b=1$. Use two Multiply nodes for $∂f/∂w=g·x$ and $∂f/∂x=g·w$, then connect $g$ directly to $∂f/∂b$. At $w=1$, $x=2$, $g=0.5$, the outputs are 1, 0.5, and 0.5.

levels.loss-intro.title: Measure the mistake
levels.loss-intro.description:
A model's answer computed from its inputs is called a prediction, written $p$; the correct answer supplied by the task is $t$. This level does not build a model or update a weight: both $p$ and $t$ are given so you can focus on comparing them.
Their difference is the error; squaring it gives squared loss $L=(p−t)²$. Drag $p$ in the plot: when $p=t$, the point reaches the bottom and loss is 0; farther from $t$, it climbs higher.
Task: build this scoring circuit with Subtract and Square, then output the loss $L$.
levels.loss-intro.hint1: Use Subtract to find the difference $p−t$. Drag $p$ past $t$ in the plot: the error changes sign, but the height still rises.
levels.loss-intro.hint2: Feed $p−t$ into Square, then into the Loss output. Squaring turns positive and negative errors into penalties no smaller than 0.
levels.3-1.title: One step downhill
levels.3-1.description:
The previous level supplied prediction $p$ and turned its error into squared loss. Its loss side now sends the upstream gradient $g=∂L/∂p$ into the model side. Build the simplest predictor $p=w·x$, then reuse the local backpropagation interface from 1-11: carry $g$ backward through the multiplication, so $∂L/∂w=g·x$.
The gradient $∂L/∂w$ points toward increasing loss; subtracting it moves toward a smaller loss. Drag $w$: the plot keeps the same hidden target while updating the supplied $∂L/∂p$, and the yellow arrow shows one step with learning rate $η=0.1$.
Task: consume the supplied $∂L/∂p$ directly, build $∂L/∂w=(∂L/∂p)·x$, then output $w′=w−0.1·∂L/∂w$.
levels.3-1.hint1: As in 1-11, start from the supplied upstream gradient instead of rebuilding the loss. Multiply $∂L/∂p$ by the local derivative $∂p/∂w=x$.
levels.3-1.hint2: Multiply the gradient by −0.1 and add it back to $w$. Your output appears as another point on the curve; it is correct when it meets the yellow arrow tip.
levels.3-2.title: How each weight should change
levels.3-2.description:
The previous construction level built one neuron with $p=w·x+b$. Here the bias is fixed at 0. The loss side has already compared the prediction with its target and supplies the scalar upstream gradient $g=∂L/∂p$; the model side must not rebuild that loss from $t$.
Reuse the local backpropagation interface from 1-11: carry $g$ backward through $p=w·x$. Multiplying the shared upstream gradient by the feature vector gives $∂L/∂w=g·x$. The weight values themselves are not needed because the local derivative $∂p/∂w$ is $x$. Broadcasting produces [3], one position per weight; as 1-10 showed, these directions form a gradient vector.
Task: multiply the supplied scalar $∂L/∂p$ by all of $x$ and output the resulting weight gradient directly. Do not attach −0.1 or update the weights; tests also use length 5. Inputs: features $x$ [3] and upstream gradient $∂L/∂p$; output: loss gradient [3].
levels.3-2.hint1: Reuse 1-11's rule $∂L/∂q=(∂L/∂p)·(∂p/∂q)$. The supplied $∂L/∂p$ is where this local backward circuit starts.
levels.3-2.hint2: Because $∂p/∂w=x$, multiply the scalar upstream gradient by all of $x$. Broadcasting produces [3], one position per weight. Connect it directly to the output without −0.1 or a weight update.
levels.3-3.title: Mean squared error
levels.3-3.description:
Display 3-1 turned one difference into squared loss $(p−t)²$. Display 2-4 built Mean. Mean squared error (MSE) combines those two ideas: compute every squared loss, then take their mean along only the last axis, keeping it at length 1. The stage diagram below follows the current values through prediction, target, difference, square, and mean.
It does not average all axes; a [2,4] test produces [2,1]. Passing unlocks Mean squared error. This level: inputs are predictions $p$ [8] and targets $t$ [8]; output loss [1] is the mean of their eight squared errors.
levels.3-3.hint1: Square each error, then average the last axis.
levels.3-3.hint2: Square differences; use Mean, keeping the last axis.
levels.3-4.title: Let it run
levels.3-4.description:
Fit a line to 16 points. Weight $w$ controls slope and bias $b$ the intercept, giving prediction $p = w·x + b$. Reuse the Linear layer from display 3-5: in this level a fresh Linear defaults to one input and one output feature, treating $x$ [16] as 16 scalar samples and producing predictions [16]. You may instead build the same formula with two scalar Parameter nodes. Feed predictions and targets into Mean squared error, then output loss.
The engine repeats forward calculation, backward gradients and parameter updates. Tune the learning rate to reach loss below 0.05 in 60 steps. Grading uses the training samples in shuffled order, with no separate test set.
This level: inputs are horizontal coordinates $x$ [16], target vertical coordinates $t$ [16]; output loss [1] is batch mean squared error, not a scalar.
levels.3-4.hint1: Connect $x$ to Linear with 1 input feature and 1 output feature, then compare its [16] predictions with $t$ using Mean squared error. Linear owns its trainable weight and bias.
levels.3-4.hint2: Manual alternative: set two Parameter shapes to scalar, multiply $x$ by $w$, and add $b$. Feed the predictions and $t$ to Mean squared error → loss. Try rate 0.1–0.5.
levels.train_diverged: Loss is higher than when training started, so training is not converging toward the goal. This is not necessarily the learning rate: first check the loss and target wiring, gradient and update direction, parameter initialization, and numerical stability. If those are correct, try a lower learning rate and reset training.
levels.train_slow: All 60 steps used and loss is still {loss}. Steps too small? Try a larger learning rate.

ui.gradHelp: Gradient of the loss with respect to this value, ∂loss/∂(·)

ui.stepPhase.backward: ② Backward: the gradient flows back from loss; each node gets ∂loss/∂(·)
ui.stepPhase.update: ③ Update: every parameter θ ← θ − η·∂loss/∂θ
levels.3-5.title: Cross entropy
levels.3-5.description:
Cross entropy rewards probability assigned to the correct class. $p$ holds class probabilities; $t$ is one-hot: 1 for the correct class, 0 elsewhere. Compute $−Σ t·ln p$ per row (Σ sums classes), then average rows. Lower correct-class probability incurs a larger penalty. The stage diagram below follows the current probabilities through logarithm, one-hot selection, per-row loss, and the batch mean. Tests change row and class counts.
This level: inputs are probabilities $p$ and labels $t$, both [4,3], one row per sample and column per class; output loss [1] is batch cross entropy.
levels.3-5.hint1: One-hot labels select the correct class. Find its negative log probability per sample, then average.
levels.3-5.hint2: Apply Logarithm to $p$, Multiply by $t$, then Sum axis −1 without keeping dimensions. Apply Mean to the resulting [4], then Negate to get [1]. For $t$ = [0,1,0], only the second class’s log probability remains.
levels.neuron.title: How one neuron predicts
levels.neuron.description:
The predictor in display 3-2 had one feature $x$ and one weight $w$. Now one sample has two features $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$, such as length and width, controlled by weights $w_{1}$ and $w_{2}$. One neuron computes:

$$
p=w_{1}x_{1}+w_{2}x_{2}+b
$$

That means multiplying each feature by its own weight, adding the results, then adding bias $b$. Written as vectors, this weighted sum is exactly a dot product, so the same calculation is $p=w·x+b$.
Stack several samples as the rows of matrix $X$, and the same calculation becomes a matrix-vector product plus bias: $Xw+b$. Each row of $X$ takes one dot product with $w$ to produce one prediction. Put several neurons' weights into matrix $W$, and this extends to the matrix multiplication $XW+b$ used later. The weights and bias are supplied inputs here, not trained.
This level: inputs are features $x$ [2], weights $w$ [2], and scalar bias $b$; output is a scalar prediction. Tests also supply 5 samples at once: $x$ [5,2] produces [5], one prediction per sample.
levels.neuron.hint1: Use the Dot product built in chapter 2 for $w·x=w_{1}x_{1}+w_{2}x_{2}$, then add $b$.
levels.neuron.hint2: For $x$ [5×2], view it as sample matrix $X$, with one sample per row. In $Xw+b$, every row takes a dot product with $w$, then scalar $b$ broadcasts across the 5 predictions.
levels.layer.title: Several neurons make a layer
levels.layer.description:
One neuron produces one prediction; several neurons can produce several scores for each sample at once. Put their weights in columns of matrix $W$ (input port $w$), with biases in vector $b$, so $xW+b$ computes them together. This 'matrix multiply plus bias' component is called a Linear layer and is added to the library when you pass.
This level: inputs are features $x$ [4,2], weights $w$ [2,3], biases $b$ [3]; output scores [4,3], one row per sample and one column per neuron.
levels.layer.hint1: $x$ [points×coords] times $W$ [coords×neurons] gives [points×neurons]. A column of $W$ is one neuron’s weights, not a row.
levels.layer.hint2: Add $b$ [neurons] to $xW$: broadcasting gives every point the same biases.
levels.3-6.title: Draw a boundary
levels.3-6.description:
Learn a straight boundary between two classes. Weight matrix $W$ [2,2] and bias $b$ [2] are trainable parameters. A linear layer computes scores $xW + b$; Softmax turns them into probabilities. The engine compares labels using cross entropy. Reach loss below 0.15 and 100% accuracy in 80 steps; grading uses a fresh set of points from the same distribution.
This level: input coordinates $x$ [40,2]; output probabilities [40,2] give each point’s two class probabilities, not loss.
levels.3-6.hint1: Add the earned Linear component, configure 2 input features and 2 output features, and connect $x$ to it. Keep bias enabled so it can learn both class scores.
levels.3-6.hint2: The configured Linear component creates and learns its own weights and bias. Connect its scores to Softmax, then output the probabilities; try learning rate 0.1.
levels.3-7.title: Remember the last step
levels.3-7.description:
Momentum accumulates gradients into a velocity, speeding updates when directions agree. With current gradient $g$ and previous momentum $m$, compute $m′ = 0.9m + g$, then update weight using $w′ = w − 0.1m′$. Both results are state for the next step: the optimizer keeps $w′$ as the new weight and $m′$ as the new momentum. This is one momentum step, not Adam.
This level: inputs are scalar weight $w$, gradient $g$, and old momentum $m$; outputs are scalar updated weight $w′$ and updated momentum $m′$.
levels.3-7.hint1: Multiply the previous momentum $m$ by 0.9, then add the new gradient $g$. Connect this $m′$ to the Updated momentum output and also reuse it for the weight update.
levels.3-7.hint2: Multiply $m′$ by 0.1 and subtract it from $w$, then connect the result to Updated weight. Both $w′$ and $m′$ are required outputs.
levels.3-8.title: Different scales, different steps
levels.3-8.description:
In 3-10, updates learned to remember past directions. The SGD option uses the plain gradient descent update from earlier: every parameter shares one learning rate. But here different parameters need different step sizes. The first data feature determines the label but is shrunk by ×0.05; the second is unrelated but enlarged by ×20. Set the learning rate low and the useful direction moves too slowly; set it high and the nuisance direction runs wild. Adam automatically adjusts the step for different parameters.
Train once with SGD, then reset the parameters, switch to Adam, and compare loss and accuracy. Reach loss below 0.15 and 100% accuracy in 600 steps. Grading uses a fresh set of points from the same distribution.
This level: input features $x$ [40,2]; output probabilities [40,2] hold two class probabilities per sample.
levels.3-8.hint1:
Configure one Linear component with 2 input features, 2 output features and bias, then connect Softmax: 

$$
Softmax(xW + b)
$$

. The network remains a linear classifier; this time you are comparing optimizers.
levels.3-8.hint2: The Linear component owns the learned $W$ [2×2] and $b$ [2]. First train with SGD at learning rate 0.05 and note the result. Then reset the parameters, switch to Adam, and train again at 0.05. Compare the two runs’ loss and accuracy.
levels.3-9.title: Bend the boundary
levels.3-9.description:
Concentric rings need more than a straight boundary. A hidden layer turns coordinates into new features; a nonlinear activation lets the second layer produce a curved decision region. $W₁$, $b₁$ are first-layer weights and biases; $W₂$, $b₂$ belong to the second. Without a nonlinear activation, both layers collapse to one linear transform plus bias.
The reference uses 16 Sigmoid hidden units. Reach loss below 0.15 and at least 95% accuracy in 300 steps. Grading uses a fresh set of points from the same distribution.
This level: input coordinates $x$ [64,2]; output probabilities [64,2] give each point’s two ring-class probabilities.
levels.3-9.hint1: Configure a Linear component from 2 input features to 16 hidden features, apply Sigmoid, then configure a second Linear from 16 features to 2 class scores. The nonlinear activation lets hidden units form new features; stacking Linear components alone is not enough.
levels.3-9.hint2: Each configured Linear component creates and learns its own weights and bias. Finish with Softmax and use Adam at 0.05; random initialization breaks hidden-unit symmetry. You may also try 8 hidden features with ReLU, then reset the model and check loss and accuracy after 300 steps.

levels.4-1.title: Characters to numbers
levels.4-1.description:
From this chapter on the network reads text. A circuit only computes with numbers, so each character first becomes an ID, say h → 0, e → 1, l → 2, o → 3.
An ID is a name, not a size: l is not “twice” e. So the network doesn’t use the ID itself; each character gets a row instead, one cell per kind of character, with 1 in its own ID’s cell and 0 elsewhere. This is one-hot encoding. With 5 kinds of characters:

$$
2 ↦ [0, 0, 1, 0, 0]
$$

This level: input idx is a run of character IDs, such as [0, 2, 4, 1]. Input k is every possible ID [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]; how many numbers it has is how many kinds of characters there are.
Output one-hot encoding: one row per character, one column per possible ID. Row i, column j is 1 exactly when the i-th ID in idx equals j. The expected one-hot encoding on the right labels its rows and columns, so you can compare.
levels.4-1.hint1: Row $i$, column $j$ answers “is the $i$-th ID equal to $j$?”. Use Insert dimension to make idx a column [4×1]; compared with $k$ [V] it broadcasts to a [4×V] table where each cell compares one pair.
levels.4-1.hint2: There is no “equals” part, but $a = b$ means “$a ≥ b$ and $b ≥ a$”. Greater or equal outputs 1 or 0; multiply the two results and only equal cells are 1.
levels.4-2.title: Look up a row
levels.4-2.description:
This level provides idx and table, but no ready-made k; One-hot still needs both idx and k. The k input must list every table row number so One-hot knows how many columns to produce. Since table [5×3] has 5 rows, first read the size of axis 0 from table, then use Range to generate k=[0,1,2,3,4].
Call the five table rows A, B, C, D, and E. Encoding ID 2 against k gives [0,0,1,0,0]. Matrix multiplication forms a weighted sum of the table rows:

$$
0A+0B+1C+0D+0E=C
$$

The zeroes remove every other row and the single 1 keeps C, so the result is exactly row 2 of table. For idx=[2,0], two one-hot rows select C and A, in that order, with one matrix multiplication.
In general, idx contains $N$ IDs and table has $V$ rows of width $D$:

$$
\operatorname{one\_hot}(idx,k)\,[N\times V] \times \mathrm{table}\,[V\times D] = \mathrm{embeddings}\,[N\times D]
$$

The default sizes are $N=4$, $V=5$, and $D=3$, giving output [4×3]. Tests change all three sizes, so derive $V$ from table instead of hard-coding 5 or k.
levels.4-2.hint1: Build k first: connect table to Dimension size with Axis set to 0 to read its row count $V$, then use Range to generate k=[0,…,$V-1$]. Do not hard-code [0,1,2,3,4], because tests change the number of table rows.
levels.4-2.hint2: Set Dimension size to axis 0 to read table's row count $V$, then connect it to Range length n to generate [0,…,$V-1$]. Feed that list as k and idx into One-hot to get [N×V], then Matrix multiply by table [V×D]. Passing unlocks Embedding, which stores table inside the component so Adam can update it during training.
levels.4-3.title: The next character
levels.4-3.description:
Now begin with the simplest sequence prediction task: look only at the current character and predict the next one. The corpus starts with little, giving adjacent training pairs l→i, i→t, t→t, t→l, and l→e. One character can have several successors, so the model outputs a probability for every candidate rather than one fixed answer.
This is not yet a sequence model with memory. It learns $P(x_{t+1}\mid x_t)$: the same current character always selects the same row of scores, regardless of anything seen earlier. Given t, for example, it cannot tell whether the preceding text was lit or cat. The later RNN chapter adds hidden state, providing a direct comparison with this memoryless baseline.
Use the Embedding unlocked by the lookup level as a trainable [V×V] score table: rows represent current characters and columns represent candidate next characters. Input ID $x$ selects one score row, Softmax turns it into probabilities, and Adam trains the table without an external table input.
After training, try continuing text with “Write”. Training and grading use every adjacent character pair in the corpus, shuffled for grading; cross entropy must be below about 2.181574. This only tests whether the model learned adjacent-character statistics, not whether it understands language or handles unseen text.
This level: $N$ is the number of character pairs and $V$ the vocabulary size. Input $x$ [N] contains current-character IDs; output probabilities [N×V] gives one row of next-character probabilities per input.
levels.4-3.hint1: Configure an Embedding with $V$ entries and embedding width $V$. Here its learned [V×V] table is a score table: rows represent current characters and columns represent possible next characters.
levels.4-3.hint2: Connect $x$ directly to the configured Embedding to select one score row per character. Apply Softmax to those scores and output the probabilities; Adam adjusts the table through cross entropy, and you can tune the learning rate.
levels.4-4.title: Draw a character
levels.4-4.description:
The previous level outputs probabilities for the next character, not one definite character. Always choosing the highest probability would produce the same result for the same input and never allow the other possibilities. Sampling chooses high-probability characters more often while still allowing less likely ones.
Use the probabilities to divide [0,1) into intervals. For p=[0.2,0.5,0.3], the interval endpoints (cumulative probabilities) are:

$$
p=[0.2,0.5,0.3] \Rightarrow c=[0.2,0.7,1]
$$

- $0≤u<0.2$: output ID 0
- $0.2≤u<0.7$: output ID 1
- $0.7≤u<1$: output ID 2

Thus $u=0.6$ lands in the second interval and outputs 1. A wider interval is hit more often, and its width is exactly that ID's probability.
In this level, build cumulative probabilities $c$ yourself. triangle contains 1 on and above its main diagonal and 0 elsewhere. Turn p into a column, multiply it element-wise by triangle, then Sum along axis 0 to obtain c. Finally, count how many interval endpoints u has passed; that count is the sampled ID.
The default inputs are probabilities p [5], uniform random scalar u, and triangle [5×5]; output one character ID (a scalar). Tests also use 8 characters, so do not hard-code the length.
levels.4-4.hint1: First compute cumulative probabilities. Use Insert dimension to turn p [V] into a column [V×1]; element-wise multiplication with triangle [V×V] then broadcasts. Row $i$ of triangle contains 1 from column $i$ onward, so probability $p_i$ is placed in column $i$ and every column to its right. Sum along axis 0, and column $j$ becomes $p_0+…+p_j$.
levels.4-4.hint2: After obtaining cumulative probabilities c, use Greater or equal to compute u≥c. For u=0.6 and c=[0.2,0.7,1], the result is [1,0,0]: the draw has passed only the first endpoint. Sum along the last axis to get 1, the sampled ID.
levels.reshape.title: Reshape
levels.reshape.description:
The next model needs two character vectors together. Practise joining them into one row without mixing samples.
For example, one sample’s vectors [1,2,3] and [4,5,6] become [1,2,3,4,5,6]. Reshape changes grouping, not value order or count. Transpose instead swaps axes.
This level: $N$ is the sample count and $D$ the character-vector length. Input $x$ [N×2×D]; output flattened values [N×2D], one row per sample. The default [2×2×3] becomes [2×6]. Tests vary $N$ and $D$, so do not hard-code them.
levels.reshape.hint1: Reshape’s Shape can contain one −1, asking the part to infer that dimension from the total value count. This differs from axis −1 meaning the last axis. Which dimension must stay unchanged?
levels.reshape.hint2: Connect $x$ to Dimension size with Axis set to 0 to get $N$. Connect that to Reshape’s Target dimension 0 and set Shape to [1, −1]. The wire sets the first dimension; the second becomes $2D$ automatically.
levels.4-5.title: One more character
levels.4-5.description:
Level 4-3 sees only the current character; this level expands the context to two consecutive characters. Looking at h alone says little about what follows, while th often precedes e and sh often precedes o. Order matters: th and ht are different contexts.
Look up a vector for each character with Embedding, join the two vectors in their original order, then feed them to an ordinary forward network that predicts the next character. This learns $P(x_{t+1}\mid x_{t-1},x_t)$. It has one more clue than the one-character model, but it still has no hidden state and carries nothing automatically into the next time step; its context length is manually fixed at 2. The next chapter's RNN reuses the same weights and carries earlier history in hidden state.
Training and grading use the same fixed 512 two-character samples, shuffled for grading. Cross entropy must be below about 1.639788; no unseen text is tested.
This level: input $x$ [512×2] contains two consecutive character IDs per row. $V$ is the vocabulary size; output probabilities [512×V] gives the candidate next-character probabilities for every row.
levels.4-5.hint1: Let $D$ be the character-vector width. Configure an Embedding with $V$ entries and width $D$, look up both characters to get [512×2×D], then join each sample into [512×2D] as in the previous level.
levels.4-5.hint2: Configure a Linear component from $2D$ input features to a hidden width, apply Tanh, then configure another Linear from that hidden width to $V$ candidate scores and apply Softmax. The lower threshold rewards learning combinations of both characters.

levels.time-rnn.title: Carry memory with one RNN step
levels.time-rnn.description:
A fixed suffix loses everything before its boundary. An RNN instead carries a hidden state from one step to the next, so later computation can use information left by earlier steps.
Project the current input and previous state to the same width, add a bias, then bound the result: $h′=tanh(xW_x+hW_h+b)$. Reusing the same weights at every step makes the model recurrent rather than a row of unrelated layers.
This level builds one step: x [B,I], h [B,H], wx [I,H], wh [H,H], b [H] → hidden state [B,H]. Defaults B/I/H are 4/2/3; tests vary them.
levels.time-rnn.hint1: Project x with wx and h with wh. Both results are [B,H], so they can be added with b.
levels.time-rnn.hint2: Compute $tanh(x·wx+h·wh+b)$. Its output becomes the previous state at the next time step.
levels.time-attention.title: Let the RNN look back
levels.time-attention.description:
Instead of forcing all evidence through one final vector, temporal attention keeps the whole hidden-state history. An explicit query is compared with every state; scaled dot products become Softmax weights, and their weighted sum returns a context vector. The query may come from the final RNN state, but the interface keeps query and history separate so later models can choose what they seek.
Inputs history [B,T,H] and query [B,H] → context [B,H]. No causal mask is needed because every entry is already observed history. Defaults B/T/H are 3/5/4; tests vary them.
levels.time-attention.hint1: Insert a length-one time axis into query, multiply by history transposed to [B,H,T], then divide scores by √H.
levels.time-attention.hint2: Softmax the T scores, multiply [B,1,T] by history [B,T,H], and reshape [B,1,H] to [B,H].
levels.time-forecast.title: Forecast the next value
levels.time-forecast.description:
Compose the complete predictor: an RNN window produces six hidden states, its final state queries temporal attention over that history, and a Linear head predicts the next scalar. Mean squared error compares the prediction with target t. Training fragments are noiseless sine waves with varied phase, frequency and amplitude; grading generates a new batch from the same ranges.
Train with Adam for 400 steps at learning rate 0.02. Held-out MSE must be below 0.02. Inputs x [16,6] and t [16]; output loss [1].
levels.time-forecast.hint1: Configure RNN window for one input feature and hidden width 8. Use its final state as Temporal attention query, then apply a Linear 8→1 head and flatten [16,1] to [16].
levels.time-forecast.hint2: Connect prediction and t to Mean squared error and output loss. Reset parameters before comparing another learning rate.
levels.5-1.title: Who should look at whom?
levels.5-1.description:
Attention scores measure relevance: query $q$ describes what to find, key $k$ what is available. $T$ counts positions and $D$ is vector width. Divide dot products by $√D$ to avoid overly sharp Softmax weights.
This level: queries $q$ and keys $k$ [T,D] → attention scores [T,T]; default [4,3] → [4,4]. A leading batch axis is also tested.
levels.5-1.hint1: Compare each query with every key to form one row of scores; obtain width from the input rather than fixing it. For query [1,0] and key [2,3], the dot product is 2, scaled to $2/√2$.
levels.5-1.hint2: Use Transpose on the last two key axes, then Matrix multiply. Dimension size gives $D$; apply Square root, then Divide the scores by it.
levels.5-2.title: Do not peek ahead
levels.5-2.description:
A causal mask prevents peeking at answers: row $i$ may read columns $j≤i$, including itself. $T$ counts positions. Keep entries on and below the diagonal; replace later entries with exactly -1e9 so Softmax gives them zero weight. Tests compare scores, not probabilities; $T$ varies.
This level: scores is a [T,T] score table; output masked scores form a table of the same shape, default [4,4]. A leading batch axis is also tested.
levels.5-2.hint1: Build the allowed region from row and column positions using Range, Insert dimension and Greater or equal. For example, row 1 can see columns 0 and 1, but not column 2; count from zero.
levels.5-2.hint2: Use Dimension size and Range to create position indices. Arrange row indices as [T,1] and column indices as [1,T]. Greater or equal gives mask $m$, with 1 where viewing is allowed. Keep the original scores multiplied by $m$; fill the other cells with −1 billion, not negative infinity.
levels.5-3.title: Mix the useful information
levels.5-3.description:
Attention mixes relevant content: $q$ is the query, $k$ the key and $v$ the value. Mask future positions, then Softmax each row into weights summing to 1. $T$ counts positions; key width $D$ and value width $E$ may differ, but their position counts must match.
This level: $q,k$ [T,D] and $v$ [T,E] → context [T,E]; default all [4,3]. A leading batch axis is also tested.
levels.5-3.hint1: First decide where to look and how much, then mix values with those weights. Each position may read itself and earlier positions. For example, weights [0.25,0.75] mix values [2,6] to give $0.25×2+0.75×6=5$.
levels.5-3.hint2: Connect Scaled attention scores → Causal mask → Softmax on the last axis → Matrix multiply by $v$.
levels.5-4.title: Give each character a position
levels.5-4.description:
Add position vectors to character vectors so the same character can differ by position.
This level: idx holds character IDs [4], tokens is the token table [7,3], positions the position table [8,3]; embeddings are position-aware vectors [4,3]. Tests vary shapes and may batch idx.
levels.5-4.hint1: Look up characters and positions separately; generate position IDs from sequence length, not character IDs. For example, the same character vector [2,3] plus position [1,0] or [0,1] becomes [3,3] or [2,4].
levels.5-4.hint2: Use Dimension size on the last idx axis, then Range for position IDs. Gather from each table and Add; position vectors broadcast across batches.
levels.5-5.title: Learn with attention
levels.5-5.description:
Train attention to predict the next character: $q$ is the query, $k$ the key, and $v$ the content to carry. Obtain them through separate projections of the same token-plus-position vectors. Project Attention outputs to vocabulary scores, then use Softmax for probabilities.
Each window contains 9 characters: the first 8 are inputs and the last 8 are targets shifted one place ahead. Position $i$ reads only itself and earlier inputs to predict character $i+1$. Training practices all 8 positions in parallel; it does not generate 8 new characters at once. Generation samples one character, appends it, then runs again.
Train with Adam for 200 steps. Training and grading use the same 128 fixed windows (shuffled for grading); cross entropy averaged over all positions must be below 1.75. This is not an independent unseen-text test.
This level: $x$ holds character IDs [128,8]; probabilities give the next-character distribution at each position [128,8,27], with a vocabulary of 27 characters.
levels.5-5.hint1: Configure Token + position embedding with 27 embeddings, maximum length 8 and embedding width 12. Feed it through three independent Linear components, each configured 12→12, to produce queries, keys and values for Attention.
levels.5-5.hint2: Configure the output Linear component 12→27 and finish with Softmax. Prediction loss trains these roles; for window little mo, the input is little m and the targets are ittle mo, so each position predicts the following character.
levels.6-1.title: Look in several ways at once
levels.6-1.description:
Multi-head attention lets channel groups choose independently where to look. $B$ counts batches, $T$ positions, and $D$ channels (vector components at each position). Split into two heads, each using $D/2$ channels for causal attention, then merge in the original order. What heads attend to is learned, not assigned by hand. Obtain sizes from inputs rather than fixing them.
This level: queries $q$, keys $k$ and values $v$ all have shape [B,T,D]; output context holds merged content with that same shape, default [2,4,8].
levels.6-1.hint1: Split channels, apply Attention independently across positions in each head, then merge. Do not attend across heads. For example, four channels [1,2,3,4] split into heads [1,2] and [3,4], each comparing positions separately.
levels.6-1.hint2: Reshape to [B,T,2,D/2], then Transpose the middle axes. Apply Attention, swap back and merge. Divide each head’s scores by $√(D/2)$; projections belong outside this component.
levels.6-2.title: Think at each position
levels.6-2.description:
Feed-forward network processes each position independently with shared weights: widen, apply ReLU, then narrow. $B,T,D,H$ denote batch, positions, input width and hidden width.
This level: vectors $x$ [B,T,D], weights w1 [D,H], w2 [H,D], biases b1 [H], b2 [D] → processed features [B,T,D]. Defaults: B=2,T=4,D=8,H=16.
levels.6-2.hint1: Widen and activate, then narrow; share weights and biases without mixing positions. For example, width 2 can expand to 4 and shrink back to 2; the number of positions stays unchanged.
levels.6-2.hint2: Use Matrix multiply and Add twice: multiply $x$ by w1, add b1, then apply ReLU. Multiply that by w2 and add b2. Biases broadcast across batches and positions.
levels.6-3.title: Attention Is All You Need
levels.6-3.description:
A Transformer block exchanges information between positions, then processes each position. Normalize before each branch and add its result to its input (a residual).
This level: vectors $x$ [B,T,D]; attention weights wq/wk/wv/wo each [D,D]; feed-forward weights w1 [D,H], w2 [H,D], biases b1 [H], b2 [D] → hidden states [B,T,D]. B/T/D/H mean batch/positions/channels/hidden width, default 2/4/8/16.
levels.6-3.hint1: Use Layer normalization before each branch, then add its result to the original branch input. Residuals preserve information and a direct gradient path; do not normalize after the addition instead. For example, adding branch result [0.1,−0.2] to input [1,2] gives [1.1,1.8].
levels.6-3.hint2: Normalize $x$, project with wq/wk/wv, use Multi-head attention, multiply by wo and add $x$ to get $h$. Apply Layer normalization to $h$, then Feed-forward network with w1/b1/w2/b2; add the result to $h$ for the hidden states.
levels.6-4.title: Let your Transformer write
levels.6-4.description:
Build a small GPT predictor: token-plus-position vectors → two Transformer blocks → Layer normalization → vocabulary projection → Softmax. Each block uses independent trainable parameters; causal attention prevents peeking ahead.
Train with Adam for 1500 steps, sampling 8 windows per step. Every 250 steps and at the end, evaluate without updates on 400 fixed windows from the same corpus. Their mean cross entropy must be below 1.1. Passing does not use the last minibatch loss or an independent test set; low loss guarantees neither fluent generation nor good predictions on new text.
Generation samples one character from the last position, appends it and runs again using trained weights without updating them.
This level: $x$ holds character IDs, [8,16] for training and [400,16] for evaluation. Output probabilities give the next-character distribution at each position, respectively [8,16,27] and [400,16,27]; the vocabulary has 27 characters.
levels.6-4.hint1: Configure Token + position embedding with 27 embeddings, maximum length 16 and embedding width 24. Then add two separate Transformer block components, each configured with feature width 24 and hidden width 48; separate blocks learn independently.
levels.6-4.hint2: After the two blocks, apply Layer normalization, configure a Linear head 24→27, and finish with Softmax. Generation draws one character at a time: after little yields a space, the next prediction reads little followed by that space.
loop.title: The training loop: five things, every step
loop.data.name: Take a batch
loop.data.fixed: The same samples every step, computed together (3-6)
loop.data.resample: A fresh random batch from the corpus every step
loop.forward.name: Forward
loop.forward.note: Compute predictions with current parameters. The level supplies data and answers; you choose wiring and parameter shapes. Training changes parameter values, not wiring or answers.
loop.loss.name: Loss
loop.loss.note: Compare predictions with answers for this step’s training batch to get a smaller-is-better number (3-5 MSE, 3-7 cross entropy). The level explains which data are graded and the loss threshold; classification levels also require accuracy.
loop.backward.name: Backward
loop.backward.note: The chain rule gives every parameter its gradient; you carried an upstream gradient by hand in 1-11, 3-2 and 3-4, now the engine does it
loop.update.name: Update
loop.update.sgd: SGD—the plain gradient descent used earlier—moves each parameter a small step against its gradient, w ← w − {lr}·gradient (3-1)
loop.update.adam: Adam: automatically adjusts the step for different parameters, base step {lr} (3-11, 3-12)
loop.repeat: Return to step 1, {steps} times in all. Lower loss means better predictions on the measured data, not necessarily on new data. Memorizing training data without handling new data is called overfitting.
coach.title: Getting started
coach.mul: This level asks for −x. The idea: multiply x by −1. First drag "Multiply" from the parts on the left onto the canvas (a click works too).
coach.wireX: Inputs are on a part's left, outputs on its right. Press on the square to the right of x, drag it to the a port on the left of Multiply, and let go.
coach.const: Now add a "Constant" and wire it to Multiply's b port. Select it and set its value to −1 under Properties on the right.
coach.wireY: Finally wire Multiply's output to y. The live values on the right then show y; compare it with "Expected" below it.
coach.run: If they match, press "Run tests" on the right: the engine checks your circuit on many values of x. Pass them all and the part is yours.

levels.time-rnn-window.title: Unroll the RNN through time
levels.time-rnn-window.description:
Use the one RNN step you built in 5-2 six times in a row, so it reads a whole sentence.
This is exactly how your RNN "read the whole sentence" on the 5-2 results page: the hidden state starts at all zeros, the 1st character updates it, the new state meets the 2nd character, and so on up to the 6th. This level lays all six steps out in front of you.
Input x [B,6] holds B sentences of 6 characters (one number each). All six steps share the same wx [1,8], wh [8,8] and b [8]. Keep every step's hidden state [B,8] and Stack them in order into a 6-row table: output [B,6,8]. Passing unlocks the RNN window component, which does all of this in one block for any sentence length.
levels.time-rnn-window.hint1: Taking character k: use Slice with axis 1, start index k, length 1 and Keep dimensions on, which gives [B,1]. Six characters means six Slices (start index 0 to 5). Feed each one into an RNN cell, wiring the same wx, wh and b into every step (in this level the RNN cell starts with automatic parameters off, so it has those ports).
levels.time-rnn-window.hint2: Chain the six cells: leave the first cell's h unconnected and it starts from an all-zero state [B,8]; every later cell takes the previous cell's output as h. Finally Stack (Inputs 6, axis 1) the six states in order into a…f to get [B,6,8].
levels.time-rnn-delay.title: Train memory over a short delay
levels.time-rnn-delay.description:
Train an RNN to remember the first number of a 6-number sequence; the other 5 numbers are small noise.
Why: this checks that the hidden state really carries early information all the way to the end — which is what let the RNN read the whole sentence.
Build: feed x into RNN window, take the last step's state with Slice (axis 1, start index -1), apply a Linear 8→1, flatten to [32], and compare with t using Mean squared error to output loss.
Then train: 300 steps; you pass when the loss is below 0.015.
levels.time-rnn-delay.hint1: Set RNN window to 1 input feature and hidden width 8. It outputs [32,6,8]; use Slice with axis 1, start index -1, length 1 and keep dims off to get the last step, [32,8].
levels.time-rnn-delay.hint2: Feed [32,8] into a Linear 8→1 to get [32,1], flatten it to [32] with Reshape, then compare with t in Mean squared error and output loss.
levels.time-recall-bottleneck.title: Expose the final-state bottleneck
levels.time-recall-bottleneck.descriptio:
Short-delay success does not remove the bottleneck: if every decision reads only the final hidden state, the entire history must fit into one fixed-width vector. The fixture contains different histories with exactly the same final state. A final-state readout must return the same query for both and therefore cannot recover which earlier path occurred.
Input history [B,T,H] → final-state query [B,H]. Defaults B/T/H are 3/5/4; tests vary them.
levels.time-recall-bottleneck.hint1: Use the time-axis length to select index T−1; do not assume T=5.
levels.time-recall-bottleneck.hint2: Select the last [B,1,H] row and sum away only the time axis to produce [B,H].
